title: Ieyasu's Portrait of Defeat
text:
In January 1573 (late 1572 in the Japanese calendar of the time), the young warlord Tokugawa Ieyasu rode out of his castle at Hamamatsu to fight the much stronger army of Takeda Shingen at Mikatagahara. It was a disaster. His army was routed, many of his retainers died covering his escape, and he barely made it back to the castle.

According to a well-known tradition, Ieyasu then had a painter make a portrait of him as he looked that day: hunched on a stool, one leg drawn up, his face twisted and exhausted with fear and defeat. He kept it, the story goes, as a reminder of his rashness and of what overconfidence had cost him, so that he would never repeat the mistake.

The painting known as the shikami portrait, the "grimacing portrait", survives in the Tokugawa Art Museum in Nagoya. Ieyasu himself went on to win at Sekigahara in 1600 and to found the Tokugawa shogunate, which governed Japan for more than two and a half centuries. He became known for patience and caution, the opposite of the young man at Mikatagahara.
lesson: Keep an honest reminder of your worst mistake where you can see it. Remembering defeat is a good guard against arrogance.
source: Tokugawa family tradition; the shikami portrait, Tokugawa Art Museum, Nagoya
caveat: Recent research suggests the link between the portrait and Mikatagahara was made long after Ieyasu's time, so the story may be modern legend.
